title: The best PSAT prep for 2026: qualifying for National Merit
summary: Comparing free tools, paid courses, and adaptive prep for the October 2026 PSAT, with a full breakdown of what it takes to qualify for National Merit.
body_markdown:
The PSAT is coming up, and many students are wondering what the best resources are to prepare and potentially qualify for the National Merit Scholarship. The PSAT/NMSQT testing window for juniors opens October 1, 2026, just over a week from now, and runs through October 30, with most schools testing on the primary date, Saturday, October 17.


This guide covers how you can best prepare for the PSAT, from free resources to paid courses to what raises a Selection Index score fast, and it's built around the goal most students searching this term actually have: qualifying for National Merit.


Take a free, full-length PSAT test to see where you stand.

## Why the PSAT is worth more than a practice run


By the time junior year approaches, many students have already taken a PSAT 8/9 or PSAT 10. Now, the PSAT/NMSQT is raising the bar. While many students still use it for practice, this is also an opportunity to qualify for the National Merit.


The College Board and National Merit Scholarship Corporation (NMSC) score the PSAT using a Selection Index: 2 times your Reading and Writing score plus your Math score (each divided by 10). Reading and Writing carries double the weight of Math, which surprises a lot of math-strong students who assume the opposite.


Out of the 1.3 to 1.5 million juniors who take the PSAT/NMSQT each year, the numbers narrow fast:


- About 50,000 students (the top 3 to 4%) earn Commended Student recognition.
- About 16,000 (the top 1% in their state) advance to Semifinalist.
- About 15,000 of those go on to Finalist standing.
- About 7,500 receive an actual scholarship.


The part that trips people up: the cutoff isn't a national number. It's set state by state, and it moves every year based on how students in that state perform, sometimes by a lot. The most recently confirmed cutoffs, released September 9, 2026, actually fell across nearly every state compared to the year before, some by 4 or 5 points, after a shift in how many students scored in the top Reading and Writing range. Check the current cutoff for your state in our[National Merit Scholarship guide](https://acely.com/psat-prep/national-merit-scholarship-guide) .


One more thing worth knowing: only your junior year PSAT/NMSQT score counts toward National Merit. Sophomore scores don't qualify, no matter how high they are. If this October is your junior year test, this is the one that matters.

## Finding the best PSAT prep for you


First it's important to focus on what will actually move a Selection Index score. This depends on where you're starting and how much time you have left. Here's a breakdown.


### Free resources (good for building the fundamentals)


**College Board and the Bluebook app.** This is non-negotiable, not optional. Bluebook is the actual testing platform, so taking a full digital practice test through it is the closest you'll get to test-day conditions, down to the adaptive format and the on-screen timing.


**Khan Academy.** Free, comprehensive, and built in partnership with the College Board, so the content lines up with what's tested. It's a solid foundation for reviewing question types across Reading and Writing and Math. The tradeoff is that it's not adaptive to your specific weak spots. Every student works through largely the same material at the same pace.


**Free tools from prep companies.** Kaplan and others offer free cram sessions, mini-courses, and sample quizzes. These are fine for spot practice, but they're built to lead into a paid course, so treat them as a preview, not a full plan.


### Paid courses (good if you need structure)


**Kaplan.** Known for on-demand courses (roughly $200) up to structured live classes (roughly $800). A reasonable option if you want a set curriculum and live instruction.


**The Princeton Review.** Leans into live instruction and detailed score analysis, with adaptive study calendars. Often positioned toward students specifically chasing National Merit qualification.


With these courses, you're paying for structure and volume, and results depend heavily on whether the program actually adapts to what you personally get wrong, or just walks every student through the same sequence. With this little time left, a program that takes a week or two to onboard you before it adapts isn't much help.

## Study books worth having on hand


The Princeton Review's PSAT/NMSQT prep book is consistently one of the better-reviewed options in test prep communities, with solid diagnostic tests and clear explanations. Treat it as a supplement to active practice, not a replacement for it, especially with limited time. Reading about a question type teaches you less than answering 50 of them and seeing what you missed.


## A realistic prep plan for whatever time you have left


The testing window opens October 1 and runs through October 30, so depending on your school's date, you might have three weeks left or three days. Either way, here's how to spend it.


**Right now:** Take one full-length practice test in Bluebook to get a real baseline score and Selection Index estimate. Compare it to your state's current cutoff so you know how big a gap you're closing.


**If you have two or more weeks:** Spend most of your time on Reading and Writing, since it's weighted double in the Selection Index. Focus specifically on the question types you missed on your baseline test, not a full review from scratch. In your final week, shift to timed, full-length practice tests to build stamina and pacing, and review every wrong answer for the reason behind it, not just the correct choice.


**If you have one week or less:** Skip broad review entirely. Spend your remaining time only on the specific question types that cost you the most points on your baseline test, and fit in one more full-length timed test if you can.


**Test week:** Ease off new material a day or two out. A short, focused review beats a last-minute cram, and it lowers the odds of walking in exhausted.


If this October isn't your qualifying year yet, the same approach applies, just start it earlier. Students who begin the summer before junior year have more time to actively prepare and raise their chances of being a National Merit semifinalist.
